Images:
  - [Image #0] The image is a tweet with a photo of a man in a green camouflage uniform walking on a sidewalk, accompanied by a lengthy text post describing his experience during an audition for "Ah Boys to Men 4." 
    
    The text, attributed to Shrey Bhargava, recounts the events that transpired during the audition. Here is the transcription of the text:
    
    "So I just finished my audition for Ah Boys To Men 4, and this is what happened inside the casting room:
    
    After completing one full take of the audition script, playing a soldier with a Singaporean accent who spoke in colloquial Singlish, I was asked by the casting director to make it 'a full blown Indian man'.
    
    Now, I get that casting directors give directions to see if actors can follow them, but really, asking me to be more Indian even after I performed the scene in a completely Singaporean way and talked as most Singaporeans would (even Indian Singaporeans)?
    
    I said "but not all Indians in Singapore speak with a thick Indian accent"
    
    And she just responded with "but that's what we want. And make it funny"
    
    So I was told to portray a caricature of my race. I was reduced to my accent, because that's what made it funny. That's what they wanted for the film. Diversity in Singaporean film, I guess comes down to playing stereotypes so the majority race can find it amusing.
    
    And also seemed as though I was just not 'Indian' enough.
    
    I wanted to decline to perform and say that they had the power to choose not to force an Indian accent on their Indian character, because that'd make them more authentically Singaporean, but I didn't. I did it. I put on a fake Indian accent and performed and it felt horrible.
    
    I left the room feeling disgusted. That was seen by my country as nothing more than the color of my skin and the way they think I ought to speak. Most Singaporean Indians I know do not speak with a full blown Indian accent, so I don't see why, a film, part of a franchise now known to be inseparably part of our national culture, needs to have an Indian character only if he is a stereotype."
    
    The text is a detailed account of the author's experience during the audition, highlighting the issues he faced with the casting director's requests and his feelings about the portrayal of Indian characters in the film.

The data contains: (1) a 2019-2021 Singapore-specific discussion about racialized language and TraceTogether privacy violations, (2) random viral tweets from 2025 about 'sharing lore,' (3) standalone reactions to unspecified trends. There is no idea evolution, no dialectic, and no cohesion between participants across time. The Singapore content shows some thematic consistency (racial politics, surveillance) but ends in 2022 with no resolution or knowledge production. The 2025 tweets are pure engagement bait with no substance. This is a classic case of 'thematic drift' where keyword overlap (snake emoji, 'trend,' 'viral') creates false connections between unrelated conversations.
